stages.title: One server. Every order goes through it
stages.desc: The shop is live and selling. Right now nothing about this looks like a problem.

stages.title: Azure has to patch the host
stages.desc: Security updates land on the physical host underneath. Your VM reboots — and it is not optional.

stages.title: Server Unavailable
stages.desc: Problem: server maintenance causes downtime. Every shopper hits an error page and leaves.

stages.title: Put two VMs in an Availability Set
stages.desc: VM1 and VM2 run the same shop. The set is Azure’s promise that it will never take both down at once.

stages.title: One address in front of both
stages.desc: Azure Load Balancer owns the public IP and health-probes each VM before it sends a single request there.

stages.title: Fault domains and update domains
stages.desc: Different rack, power and switch. And Azure only ever reboots one update domain at a time.

stages.title: Requests start arriving
stages.desc: Shoppers hit one public address. They have no idea how many servers are behind it.

stages.title: The load balancer splits the traffic
stages.desc: Roughly half to VM1, half to VM2 — and it keeps probing both the entire time.

stages.title: Both green. Orders going through
stages.desc: Two servers doing the work of one. The spare capacity is a bonus, not the point.

stages.title: Azure starts maintenance on VM1
stages.desc: Update domain 0 goes first. VM1 drains and reboots — update domain 1 is not touched.

stages.title: Traffic Automatically Redirected
stages.desc: The health probe fails, the load balancer drops VM1 from the pool, and VM2 takes 100%.

stages.title: The shopper never finds out
stages.desc: Same URL, same cart, same checkout. No error page, no support ticket, no abandoned basket.

stages.title: VM1 rejoins. Only then does UD 1 go
stages.desc: The probe passes, traffic rebalances — and Azure waits for that before touching VM2 at all.

stages.title: High Availability Achieved
stages.desc: Two VMs, one availability set, one load balancer. Azure backs it with a 99.95% SLA.

end.title: Azure reboots the server. Your shop keeps selling
end.sub: An availability set spreads your VMs across fault and update domains, so planned maintenance takes one out at a time while the load balancer sends every shopper to the other.

post.caption:
A shop running on one VM. Azure schedules a security patch on the host, the VM reboots, and every shopper gets "Server Unavailable".

That is not a technical incident. It is abandoned carts, refund requests, and a screenshot of your error page circulating long after the server came back.

An Azure Availability Set fixes it at deploy time, and it costs nothing — you pay only for the VMs.

Put VM1 and VM2 in the same availability set and Azure spreads them across:
• Fault domains — separate rack, separate power feed, separate network switch. A rack failure cannot take both.
• Update domains — separate patch groups. During planned platform maintenance Azure reboots one update domain at a time and waits (roughly 30 minutes) before starting the next.

Front them with Azure Load Balancer. It health-probes each VM continuously. When VM1 goes down for its patch the probe fails, the load balancer pulls VM1 out of the backend pool, and VM2 absorbs 100% of the traffic. Nobody gets paged. Nobody edits DNS. The shopper checking out never sees anything.

The SLA follows the design: 99.95% for two or more VMs in an availability set, against 99.9% for a single VM on premium storage.

The catch worth knowing: an availability set protects you inside one datacenter — rack failures, host failures, planned maintenance. It does not protect you if the whole datacenter goes. That is what Availability Zones are for, and they take you to 99.99%.

And your VMs still share nothing. If session state lives in a web server's memory, half your shoppers get logged out on failover anyway.

How many of your production VMs are running alone right now?
